entities.name: De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Published in 1543 by Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), a Polish canon and mathematician, De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium (On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres) proposed that the Earth revolves around the Sun — overturning the Ptolemaic geocentric model that had dominated Western astronomy for over 1,400 years. Copernicus developed his theory over decades at Frombork in Royal Prussia, presenting a mathematically rigorous (if complex) alternative to Ptolemy's Almagest.

The work was published just before Copernicus's death — legend holds he received the first printed copy on his deathbed. Although its immediate impact was limited (an unauthorized preface by the theologian Osiander cautiously described the heliocentric model as merely a mathematical convenience), the Copernican Revolution it initiated fundamentally altered humanity's self-understanding.

It dislodged Earth — and by implication humanity — from the center of the cosmos, provoking what Freud later called the first of three great "narcissistic wounds" to human self-regard. Kepler and Galileo built upon Copernicus's foundation to complete the astronomical revolution.
